strengths: Novel problem formulation distinguishing intent discovery from intent elicitation, well-grounded in cognitive science
Creative hierarchical intent simulator with automatic tree construction from artifacts enabling domain generalization
Comprehensive experimental validation including simulated evaluation, real user study with 75 participants, generalization testing, and behavioral analysis

Meaningful empirical improvements: 10-13% intent discovery gain, 84% user satisfaction (vs 72-78% baselines), 27-44% conversation reduction, consistent pattern of better divergence-convergence balance
Solid technical execution with multiple training paradigms (SFT/DPO/GRPO), thoughtful reward design, and proper handling of user expressiveness constraints
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendices including all prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details
Honest discussion of limitations including simulator assumptions, safety risks, and low absolute satisfaction scores with appropriate safety evaluation
weaknesses: User simulator fidelity not deeply validated: intent hierarchies extracted via LLM prompting without human verification of whether they capture real preferences; tangential engagement uses random thresholds with no reported variance
Low absolute performance limits practical impact: only 28-40% satisfaction scores across settings; unclear whether this is task-inherent or framework-fixable

Evaluation methodology concerns: using LLM judges (GPT-5.1) for satisfaction/interactivity introduces error; discovery score normalization (Eq. 4) excludes easy/hard cases making absolute progress assessment difficult
Limited generalization evidence: only 10 artifacts per task type; mixed results with underperformance on data visualization; small total sample (50 examples)

Ad-hoc design choices: random threshold sampling for tangential engagement lacks justification; Equation 5 uses fixed p=0.25 without sensitivity analysis; efficiency penalty cap at 1 not well motivated
Potential circular reasoning: training data generated with reward function; evaluation uses same function to judge success
Experimental limitations: 5-turn conversations are short; COLLABLLM baseline from concurrent work; no ablation studies on reward components; prompted baseline inconsistent across models

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly distinguishes intent discovery from intent elicitation with compelling examples grounded in cognitive science
Novel user simulator: Hierarchical intent trees with progressive discovery states is an intuitive and creative approach to operationalize intent discovery for scalable training
Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (3 domains), models (2 base models), metrics, generalization tests, and user study with 75 participants
Empirical improvements: 10-13% discovery gains, 27-44% conversation length reduction, balanced behavioral patterns (divergence/convergence)
User study validation: Crucially, real users confirm that simulated improvements transfer to actual preferences
Honest limitations discussion: Section 2.3 transparently acknowledges monotonic refinement and expressiveness constraints
weaknesses: CRITICAL: User simulator validity unvalidated - Entire framework depends on Gemini-based evaluation of intent engagement with zero human verification. No correlation study between LLM judgments and actual intent discovery. The evaluator's limited view (only first root with undiscovered descendant) is never validated for accuracy

CRITICAL: Intent satisfaction crisis - Satisfaction scores are only 30-37% despite 42-45% discovery. This large gap contradicts the framework's central premise. Paper acknowledges but doesn't investigate whether this indicates simulator misalignment or fundamental infeasibility within 5 turns, undermining practical utility

Intent tree quality completely unvalidated - Automatically generated hierarchies (via Claude) are never compared to human annotations. Figure 6 shows one example. No ablation on tree quality impact. Artifacts themselves (r/WritingPrompts) may introduce selection bias

Insufficient ablations on critical design choices - (1) Reward additive combination lacks justification; (2) Tangential engagement mechanism (Eq. 5) with random thresholds p=0.25, θv~[0,1] has no sensitivity analysis; (3) No ablation separating direct vs. tangential engagement contributions; (4) No ablation validating that discovery reward improves over baseline SFT

All evaluation metrics depend on LLM judges creating circularity - Discovery Score normalized to exclude trivial/unreachable cases reduces interpretability. Intent Satisfaction uses GPT-5.1-as-judge (no correlation study). Interactivity uses LLM judgment of collaboration. No human evaluation of results quality

Weak baseline comparisons - COLLABLLM designed for elicitation not discovery (unfair comparison). Prompted base shows inconsistent results (helps Qwen, hurts Llama) suggesting model-dependency. Missing ablation: does the discovery reward actually help vs. pure SFT?
Limited generalization - Only 10 artifacts per task type in generalization test (underpowered). Negative transfer on data visualization (-1%). Mixed results; claim of generalization overstated

User study lacks statistical rigor - n=75 only, limited to writing tasks, no significance testing reported, no power analysis, qualitative feedback is anecdotal. Some participants found options 'overwhelming' and 'standardised' suggesting current approach has known issues
Safety evaluation acknowledged as limited - Only 3 benchmarks. Doesn't directly test stated risk: models susceptible to exploring vague harmful requests. The specific concern remains untested

Missing error analysis and failure investigation - Only one positive case study; no systematic analysis of when/why approach fails. No discussion of failure modes or intent types that resist discovery

strengths: Clear problem formulation distinguishing intent discovery from intent elicitation, well-motivated with compelling examples and grounded in cognitive science literature
Novel and technically sound hierarchical user simulator with automated intent tree construction, enabling scalable application across diverse domains
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning three domains, multiple metrics, proper baselines, normalized scoring, and generalization testing to unseen tasks
Human validation with 75 participants showing improvements transfer from simulation to real users, with qualitative feedback confirming the core premise
Strong behavioral analysis (Figure 3) demonstrating balanced divergence-convergence patterns in trained models vs. baseline fixation
Honest limitations discussion (Section 2.3) and safety evaluation (Appendix D) showing no degradation in safety scores despite collaborative training
High reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, prompts, cost analysis, and sufficient detail for implementation
Well-written with clear presentation, effective visualizations, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: User simulator design choices feel ad-hoc: tangential engagement scoring (Eq. 5) lacks theoretical justification, random threshold sampling not validated, and cumulative score mechanism empirically motivated without ablations
Critical missing ablations on reward components (discovery/efficiency weighting), tangential engagement mechanism, discovery state definitions, and sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters

Intent tree construction quality not validated: no comparison with human-created trees, no inter-annotator agreement metrics, no error analysis of LLM failures, and this critical pipeline input entirely depends on Claude Sonnet correctness
Modest absolute satisfaction scores (30-38% across conditions) suggest discovered intents still difficult to satisfy within 5 turns, reducing practical utility despite improved discovery rates
Limited scope to open-ended creative/design tasks only; unclear if intent discovery framing applies to closed-ended tasks (math, QA), significantly limiting generalization claims

Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests, some improvements modest (SVG Qwen3-8B: 4%), only 3 repetitions per conversation, making it impossible to assess which gains are significant

Multiple LLM dependencies introduce brittleness: Claude for trees, Gemini for evaluation, GPT-5.1 for satisfaction and interactivity scoring; no analysis of judge reliability or potential cascading errors

CollabLLM baseline underperforms partly due to user simulator design (penalizes clarifying questions users can't answer); limited comparison with other multi-turn optimization and recent collaborative dialogue work
Training/test data from same sources (WritingPrompts, journalistic articles) with small separation (500 train + 100 test) raises data leakage concerns

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly-formulated problem distinguishing intent discovery from elicitation, grounded in cognitive science literature
Comprehensive experimental validation including simulated evaluation across 3 domains, 5 new domains for generalization, real user study (75 participants), and extensive ablations
Consistent improvements across models and domains (~10% relative improvement in discovery, 32% conversation reduction, 83% interactivity improvement)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed appendices covering all prompts, hyperparameters, intent tree construction, and conversation simulation procedures
Novel operationalization of intent discovery through hierarchical intent trees with response-driven progressive refinement
Strong ethical considerations including safety evaluation, honest discussion of assumptions, and proper human participant treatment
Behavioral analysis demonstrating learned divergence/convergence patterns validate that models discover the intended collaborative strategy
weaknesses: Core assumptions are restrictive (monotonic refinement violated 5.3%, single-dimension focus violated 14.7%) and their impact on real tasks not thoroughly analyzed
Heuristic simulator design choices lack theoretical grounding: tangential engagement uses arbitrary random thresholds from [0,1], fixed probability p=0.25 lacks sensitivity analysis
Intent tree construction via LLM achieves only ~85.7% aspect consistency; the ~15% imperfect pairs could introduce systematic biases into training/evaluation, not analyzed
Simplistic reward design treats all intents equally (R_d = |I_{t+1}| - |I_t|) ignoring difficulty/importance; efficiency penalty capping lacks justification
Modest absolute performance: best discovery ~45-48%, intent satisfaction ~33-38%, limiting practical applicability despite consistent relative gains
Limited scope: all three domains are generative/creative; generalization to reasoning, analytical, or non-creative tasks remains unexplored
Reliance on LLM judges (GPT-5.1) for intent satisfaction without inter-annotator agreement reporting; potential biases not addressed
Technical novelty is incremental, building straightforwardly on existing components (hierarchical trees, simulators, SFT/RL); the key novelty is the latent intent concept
User study is limited in scale (75 participants, creative writing only, ~8 turns per interaction) though results do validate simulation findings
Cross-domain generalization test uses only 10 artifacts per task type, which is quite small for strong claims

strengths: Well-motivated problem grounded in cognitive science literature—distinguishes intent discovery from intent elicitation, an important and underexplored distinction
Comprehensive experimental validation including simulated experiments with multiple ablations, human study with 75 participants, and generalization tests on unseen domains
Technically sound formalization with clear problem setup and reasonable hierarchical intent operationalization
Extensive reproducibility support through detailed appendix with all prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details; human validation of intent trees (85.7% consistency)
Behavioral analysis (Figure 3) showing models learn appropriate diverge/converge patterns demonstrates the framework captures meaningful collaborative behavior
Includes human study validation confirming simulated improvements transfer to real users with statistical significance
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is applying established cognitive science concepts via standard hierarchical intent simulator—more an application than fundamental innovation for ML conference

Modest empirical improvements: 10-14% on normalized discovery metrics with low absolute performance (discovery ~40-50%, satisfaction ~30-37%); user study shows only ~4-12% satisfaction rating improvement
Artificial simulator assumptions inadequately justified: monotonic refinement (5.3% violation), single-dimension focus (14.7% violation), and response-only intent discovery lack empirical grounding

Ad-hoc design choices without principled justification: tangential engagement uses random thresholds (θv ~ Uniform[0,1]), reward function capping feels engineered; paper admits normalizing Rd yields inconsistent signals but provides no evidence

Evaluation tied to simulator: Intent Discovery Score normalizes by per-instance bounds obscuring absolute performance; Intent Satisfaction uses LLM-as-judge introducing variance; custom metrics may not transfer to real-world intent satisfaction
Mixed generalization: DISCOVERLLM underperforms on data visualization task (Table 2: 54.4% vs. 59.4% baseline), questioning robustness across domains

Limited baseline comparisons: only Base, Prompted Base, and COLLABLLM; Prompted Base shows inconsistent results (helps Qwen, hurts Llama); no comparison to other multi-turn interactive or intent discovery approaches

Intent tree construction relies on LLM outputs with ~15% error rate; impact on training unquantified; non-deterministic outputs complicate reproduction; cost ($0.189 per conversation) limits scalability
Low absolute satisfaction scores (~30-37%) indicate framework addresses discovery but not downstream satisfaction—the stated problem remains partially unsolved
Safety evaluation acknowledged as limited in scope; behavioral assumptions (monotonic refinement, single-dimension) violated in 5-14% of real user study conversations

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Clearly distinguishes intent discovery (helping users form preferences) from intent elicitation (extracting pre-formed intents), addressing an under-studied challenge motivated by cognitive science
Thoughtful system design: The hierarchical intent representation with progressive concretization and three-stage discovery states elegantly captures how users form preferences through exploration

Comprehensive experimental validation: Rigorous evaluation across three diverse domains, unseen task generalization, multiple metrics (discovery/satisfaction/interactivity), simulator configuration ablations, and independent benchmark evaluations

Strong reproducibility: All LLM prompts provided, detailed hyperparameters, human validation of intent tree quality (85.7%), and assumption verification on real data (monotonic refinement holds 94.7%)
Real user study confirmation: 75-participant study validates simulated improvements, with participants noting the model 'anticipated' their latent intents, confirming practical utility
Honest limitations discussion: Explicitly states simplifying assumptions, validates them empirically, acknowledges low satisfaction scores, and discusses potential safety risks
weaknesses: Low absolute satisfaction scores (27-37% across tasks) raise concerns about practical utility—users may still be frustrated even with improved discovery. While acknowledged, this significantly limits real-world applicability

Ad-hoc simulator design choices: Random uniform thresholds for tangential engagement (Eq. 5), single-dimension focus restriction, and best-alternative evaluation rule lack full justification or sensitivity analysis

Limited baseline strength: COLLABLLM is somewhat inherently misaligned (trained for clarification, not discovery). Prompted baselines show inconsistent results. No comparison to discovery-optimized alternatives

Evaluation metrics limitations: Intent Discovery normalization makes absolute scores context-dependent and hard to interpret (what does 45% discovery mean?). LLM-as-a-judge introduces potential bias. Only end-of-conversation measurement misses discovery trajectories
Modest empirical improvements: ~10% discovery gain, ~11% satisfaction gain across substantial added complexity. ROI and significance (especially in user study) unclear without statistical tests

Limited scope and generalization: All three main tasks are creative/design domains. Generalization to factual QA, code generation, or information-seeking tasks is unexplored. Unseen tasks still similar in nature
Incomplete failure mode analysis: Case study shows only success. No documented failures, analysis of when DISCOVERLLM underperforms, or investigation of what makes effective discovery options

User study limitations: Small sample (75), no significance testing, crowdworker-only population, writing tasks only, short average duration (15 min). Unclear how findings transfer to other populations and task types
Simulator design bias not addressed: Intent trees constructed with Claude/Gemini. Sensitivity to tree construction method not tested (B.8 tests simulator backbone but not tree generation)
Missing computational analysis: No comparison of computational cost versus baselines despite $0.189 per synthetic conversation and multi-API requirements
